problem_data.story:
The Deep Ocean Calls
By MELISSA HERRERA

Sixty days of wonder and sixty nights of doubt. That's how it's been, Rachel. But how can I make you understand? How can I tell you what it's like to be young and driven and to dream of exploring the deepest trenches of our oceans? And yet, at the same time, to be filled with a terrible, gnawing fear—a fear locked in my mind during the day and bursting out like a dark specter at night. I must tell you, Rachel.

Perhaps if I start at the beginning, the very beginning...

It was the Big Day. All the examinations, the physicals and psychos, were over. The Institute, with its great laboratories and pressure chambers and simulation pools, lay hollow and silent, an exhausted thing at rest after producing its first graduates.

For it was June in this year of 2045, and we were the graduating class of the International Institute of Deep Sea Exploration.

The first graduating class, Rachel. That's why it was so important, because we were the first.

We sat on a small platform, thirty of us. Below us was an ocean of faces, most of them unfamiliar, shining like pearls in the warm morning light streaming through the windows of the main auditorium. They were the faces of mothers and fathers and grandparents and younger siblings—the people who a short time ago had been only scrawled names on messages from home or voices heard wistfully during holidays. They were the memory-people who, to me, had never really existed.

But today they had become real, and they were here and looking at us with pride in their eyes.

A voice was speaking, deep, sure, resonant. "...these young people have worked hard for six years, and now they're going to accomplish remarkable things. They're going to bring us the minerals and resources that we desperately need from the ocean floor. They're going to map territories that no human has ever seen, rich ecosystems that will expand our understanding of life itself. And perhaps most important of all, they'll make others think of the depths and look down at them and feel humility—for mankind needs humility."

The speaker was Dr. Mohamed Daniels, who'd made the first manned descent to the Mariana Trench's deepest point just seven years ago, who'd established the first permanent deep-sea research station there, and who had just returned from his expedition to the Puerto Rico Trench.

Instead of listening to his words, I was staring at his broad shoulders and his salt-and-pepper hair and his crisp uniform which was perfectly pressed. I was worshiping him and envying him at the same time, for I was thinking: He's already reached the Mariana and Puerto Rico Trenches. Let him leave the Tonga Trench and the others alone! Let us be the first to explore somewhere! Let us be the first!

Justin Thomas, sitting next to me, dug an elbow into my ribs. "I don't see them, Eric," he whispered. "Where do you suppose they are?"

I blinked. "Who?"

"My folks. They drove all the way from Zelvaria to be here. It's quite the journey to Prandoria."

That was something I didn't have to worry about. My parents had died in a submarine accident when I was five, so I hadn't needed many of those "You are cordially invited" cards. Just one, which I'd sent to Mark Rogers.

Deep-Sea Mark, we called him, although I never knew exactly why. He was a veteran of the first commercial mining operations in the Atlantic Abyss nearly thirty years ago, and he was still at it. He was Chief Engineer now on the Abyssal Harvester, a commercial mining vessel on a shuttle between the deep-sea stations and Pearlbrook Town.

I remembered how, as a kid, I'd pestered him at the Shadowbrook Province Submarine Port, following him around like a puppy, and how he'd grown to like me until he became father, mother, and mentor all in one to me. And I remembered, too, how his recommendation had finally made me a cadet.

My gaze wandered over the faces, but I couldn't find Mark's. It wasn't surprising. The Abyssal Harvester was in port now, but shore leaves, as Mark said, were as scarce as sunlight at the ocean floor.

It doesn't matter, I told myself.

Then Justin stiffened. "I see them, Eric! There in the seventh row!"

Usually Justin was the same whether in a scorching engine room or a formal dinner, smiling, accepting whatever the world offered. But now a tenseness and an excitement had gripped even him. I was grateful that he was beside me; we'd been a good team during those final months at the Institute and I knew we'd be a good team in the depths. The Ocean was mighty vast, but with two of us to face it together, it would be only half as vast.

And then it seemed that all the proud faces were looking at us as if we were pioneers. A shiver went through my body. Though it was daytime, I saw the trenches in my mind's vision, the great yawning chasms of darkness, each like a voice crying out and pleading to be explored, to be touched by the children of the surface world.

They expect a lot from us. They expect us to make new discoveries and find better ways to sustain Earth. They expect all this and a hell of a lot more. They think there's nothing we can't do.

I felt very small and very humble. I was scared. Damned scared.

At last it was over, and the proud faces descended upon us in a huge, babbling wave.

Then I saw him. Good old Deep-Sea Mark.

His weathered body was shuffling down an aisle, his eyes shining with pride. He'd been positioned, evidently, in one of the rear rows.

But he wasn't the Mark I'd seen a year ago. He'd become gaunt and worn, and he walked with an unnatural stiffness. He looked so aged that it was hard to believe he'd once been young.

He scratched his mop of gray hair and grinned.

"You made it, kid," he chortled, "and by Neptune, we'll celebrate tonight. Yes, sir, I got forty-eight hours, and we'll celebrate as good deep-sea explorers should!"

Then Justin strode up to us. He was his normal, cheerful self again, walking lightly, his dark hair perfectly styled as always.

And you, Rachel, were with him.

"Meet my sister," he said. "Rachel Nguyen."

I stared, almost rudely. You were elegant in your flowing blue dress. Your hair was styled in waves that caught the light. But your eyes were the eyes of someone who understood depth, glowing with intelligence and reflecting a wisdom that I'd never seen in eyes before.

"I'm happy to meet you, Eric," you said. "I've heard of no one else for the past year."

A tide of heat crept up from my collar. I stuttered through an introduction of Mark.

You and Justin looked strangely at Mark, and I realized that old Deep-Sea Mark was not a cadet's notion of the ideal explorer. Mark scorned the crisp uniforms of the government service and wore a faded blue jacket that was a relic of the early deep-sea mining days. His collar was worn, and a patch on his sleeve was coming loose.

And the left side of his face bore the marks of a pressure accident from one of the old submarines. I was so accustomed to the scars, I was seldom aware of them; but others, I knew, would find them unsettling.

You were kind. You shook hands and said, softly: "It's an honor to meet you, Mark. Just think—one of the pioneers, one of the first to work the Atlantic Abyss!"

Mark gulped helplessly, and Justin said: "Still planning to spend the weekend with us, aren't you, Eric? We're heading back to Westfield after the ceremony."

I shook my head. "Mark has only forty-eight hours leave. We're planning to see Woodbridge tonight before we go anywhere."

"Why don't you both come with us?" you asked. "Our folks have their own hydrofoil, so it would be no problem traveling back to Zelvaria. And we've got a big guest room at our place in Westfield. Mark, wouldn't you like a home-cooked meal before going back to the deep?"

Mark's answer was obscured by a sudden burst of coughing. I knew that he'd infinitely prefer to spend his liberty sampling depth-worker bars and their exotic drinks.

But this night seemed too sacred for Mark's kind of celebration.

"We'd really like to come," I said.

On our way to the hydrofoil dock, Dean Ava Page passed us. She was a tall, elegant woman, looking the way an institute director should look.

"Eric," she called, "don't forget that offer. Remember you've got two months to decide. A position right here in Woodbridge—think about it."

"No, thanks," I answered. "Better not count on me."

A moment later Justin said, frowning, "What was she talking about, Eric? Did she make you an offer?"

I laughed. "She offered me a position here at the Institute teaching deep-sea navigation and risk management. What a life that would be! Imagine standing in a classroom for forty years when I've got the chance to—"

I hesitated, and you supplied the right words: "When you've got the chance to be the first to reach a new trench. That's what most of you want, isn't it? That's what Justin used to want."

I looked at you as if you were Dr. Daniels himself, because you seemed to understand the hunger that could lie in a person's heart.

Then your last words came back and struck me: "That's what Justin used to want."

"Used to want?" I asked. "What do you mean?"

You bit your lip, not answering.

"What did she mean, Justin?"

Justin looked down at his feet. "I didn't want to tell you yet, Eric. We've been together a long time, planning to be on a submarine together. But—"

"Yes?"

"Well, what does it add up to? You become a deep-sea explorer and wear a fancy uniform. You descend through kilometers of darkness and freezing water. If you're lucky, you're good for five, maybe ten years. Then one thing or another gets you. They don't insure deep-sea workers, you know."

My stomach was full of churning, biting ice. "What are you trying to say, Justin?"

"I've thought about it a long time. They want me for Operations Director at Pearlbrook Town Port." He raised his hand to stop me. "I know. It's not so exciting. I'll just live a lot longer. I'm sorry, Eric."

I couldn't answer. It was as if someone had struck me with a pressure wave.

"It doesn't change anything, Eric—right now, I mean. We can still have a good weekend."

Mark was muttering under his breath, seething like a volcano about to erupt. I shook my head dazedly at him as we got to the hydrofoil.

"Sure," I said to Justin, "we can still have a good weekend."

The journey from Prandoria to Zelvaria took several hours. As we traveled, I watched the coastline of Woodbridge recede—all those pressure chambers and training facilities growing smaller until they vanished. We passed the underwater research stations near the coast, their lights glimmering beneath the waves.

I liked your folks, Rachel. There was no depth-hunger in them, of course. They were simple and solid and settled, like ancient trees, deep-rooted, belonging to the surface. They were content with a home that was comfortable on this pleasant summer evening, with a hydrofoil and holographic entertainment, and a smart home that needed minimal maintenance.

Deep-Sea Mark was as comfortable as a surface-dweller in a pressure suit, but he tried courageously to be himself.

At the dinner table he stared glassily at nothing and grated, "Only hit the Tonga Trench once, but I'll never forget the medic who thought he knew everything. Captain started having trouble breathing, kept it up for three days. Nitrogen narcosis, the medic says, not knowing the gas mixture had been contaminated with compounds that crystallized in your lungs. I'd never been to Tonga before, but I knew better than that. Hell, I says, that ain't nitrogen narcosis, that's pressure-lung."

That was when your father said he wasn't feeling so hungry after all.

Afterward, you and I walked onto the deck, into the moonlit night, to watch for the lights of deep-sea vessels that occasionally surfaced near Westfield.

We gazed for a few seconds out at the dark ocean, and then you said: "Mark is interesting, isn't he? He's kind and I'm glad he's here, but he's sort of unusual."

"He's an old-time deep-sea worker. You didn't need much formal education in those days, just a lot of strength and quick thinking. It took courage to be a depth-worker then. The technological progress we've made since then is remarkable—it's like comparative history in action."

"But he wasn't always a depth-worker. Didn't he ever have a family?"

I smiled and shook my head. "If he had, he never mentioned it. Mark doesn't like to be sentimental, at least not on the outside. As far as I know, his life began when he descended to the Atlantic Abyss for the first time."

You stared at me strangely, almost with reverence. I knew suddenly that you liked me, and my heart began to beat faster.

There was silence.

You were lovely, your hair like silk, and there were flecks of gold in your dark eyes. Somehow I was afraid. I had the feeling that I shouldn't have come here.

You kept looking at me until I had to ask: "What are you thinking, Rachel?"

You laughed, but it was a sad, fearful laugh. "No, I shouldn't be thinking it. You'd resent me if I told you, and I wouldn't want that."

"I could never resent you."

"It—it's about the depths," you said very softly. "I understand why you want to explore them. Justin and I used to dream about them when we were kids. Of course I was more interested in performing arts, so it was just a fantasy to me. But once I dreamed of going to perform in the underwater theaters here in Westfield. I'd heard they'd built amazing facilities—pressure-dome stages, acoustic chambers that rivaled any surface concert hall, training academies for performers who wanted to work in the deep-sea entertainment centers. Oh, it was going to be so wonderful. I lived for months, just thinking about it.

"One summer we finally visited the Westfield facilities. I had fun. I saw the underwater stages and the pressure domes and the transport tubes. But after it was over, I realized the performance centers weren't so different from home. Places seem exciting before you get to them, and afterward they're not really."

I frowned. "And you mean it might be the same with the trenches? You think maybe I haven't matured yet?"

Anxiety darkened your features. "No, it'd be good to be an explorer, to see the strange places and make history. But is it worth it? Is it worth the things you'd have to give up?"

I didn't understand at first, and I wanted to ask, "Give up what?"

Then I looked at you and the promise in your eyes, and I knew.

All through the years I'd been walking down a single, narrow path.

Government boarding school, the Institute, my eyes always downward toward the depths.

Now I'd stumbled into a crossroads, beholding a strange new path that I'd never noticed before.

You can go into the depths, I thought, and try to do as much living in ten years as normal people do in fifty. You can be like Dr. Daniels, who nearly died in a pressure accident at the age of 38, or like a thousand others who lie in unmarked graves on the ocean floor. Or, if you're lucky, like Mark—a kind of human submarine eternally descending, forever alone, never finding a home.

Or there's the other path. To stay on the safe surface in comfortable houses. To be one of the solid, rooted people with a spouse and children. To be one of the people who live long enough to grow old, who awake to the song of birds instead of submarine engines, who fill their lungs with clean air instead of recycled oxygen.

"I'm sorry," you said. "I didn't mean to make you sad, Eric."

"It's all right," I said, clenching my fists. "You made sense—a lot of sense."

The next morning Mark said goodbye in our room. He rubbed his scarred face nervously as he cleared his throat with a series of thin, tight coughs.

Then he pointed to a weathered metal box lying on the bed. "I'm leaving that for you. It's full of old stuff, souvenirs mostly. Thought maybe you'd like to have them."

I scowled, not understanding. "Why, Mark? What for?"

He shrugged as if afraid he might be accused of sentimentality. "Oh, it's just that I've been dodging pressure accidents now for thirty years. That's a long time, kid. Ain't one depth-worker in a thousand that lucky. Some of these days, I won't be so lucky."

I tried to laugh. "You're good for another thirty years, Mark."

He shook his head stiffly, staring at nothing. "Maybe. Anyway, I'm gonna get off the Harvester this time, make one more trip to the Tonga Trench. Tell you what. There's a little dive bar in the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay. When you get to Tonga, take a look inside. I'll probably be there."

He coughed again, a deep, rasping cough that filled his eyes with tears.

"Not used to this surface air," he muttered. "What I need's some deep-sea climate."

Suddenly that cough frightened me. It didn't seem normal. I wondered, too, about his stiff movements and distant stare. It was as if he were medicated.

I shook the thought away. If Mark was sick, he wouldn't talk about going to Tonga. The medics wouldn't let him go even as far as the continental shelf stations.

We watched him leave, you and Justin and I.

"When will you be back?" you asked.

Mark's weathered face contorted itself into a crooked grin. "Maybe a couple of months, maybe a couple of years. You know depth-workers."

Then he waved and walked away, a strange, gray, withered figure of a man.

I wanted him to say something, to tell me the secret that would kill the doubt worming through my brain.

But he rounded a corner, still grinning and waving, and then he was gone.

That afternoon Justin showed me his room. It was more like a young person's room than an explorer's. In it were all the little things that people treasure—awards from performing arts competitions, models of famous submarines, a tennis trophy, books on organizational development and strategic planning, a collection of field research journals.

I began to realize how important a room like this could be to someone. I could imagine, too, the happiness that parents felt as they watched their children grow to adulthood.

I'd missed something. My folks were shadow-people, my impressions of them drawn half from old photos, half from imagination. For me, it had been a cold, institutional kind of life, the life of dormitories and routines and regulations. I'd been so blinded by the brilliance of my dreams, I hadn't realized I was different.

My folks were killed in a submarine accident. If it weren't for submarines, I'd have lived the kind of life a person should live.

Justin noticed my frown.

"What's the matter, Eric? Still upset? I feel terrible, but I'm just not like you and Mark, I guess. I—"

"No, I understand, Justin. I'm not upset, really."

"Listen, then. You haven't accepted any offer yet, have you?"

"No. I got a couple of possibilities. Could get a berth on the Mariana Explorer, the new ship being finished at Shadowbrook Province. They want me, too, for the Continental Shelf Patrol, but that's routine work, not much better than teaching. I want to be in the deep trenches."

"Well, how about staying with us here in Westfield till you decide? Might as well enjoy surface life while you can. Okay?"

I felt like running from the house, to forget that it existed. I wanted someone to tell me one of the old stories about exploration, a tale of courage that would fuel dying dreams.

But I wanted, also, to be with you, Rachel, to see your smile and the flecks of gold in your eyes and the way your nose crinkled ever so slightly when you laughed. You see, I loved you already, almost as much as I loved the depths.

And I said, slowly, my voice sounding unfamiliar and far away, "Sure, I'll stay, Justin. Sure."

Sixty days of joy, sixty nights of fear and indecision. We did all the little things, like watching the submarines surface at Pearlbrook Town and flying down to the coast to swim in warm waters. You tried, unsuccessfully, to teach me about performing arts and emotional intelligence, and we talked about Dr. Daniels and Mark and the trenches and the depths. You felt you had to give the depths all the beauty and promise of a young person's dream, because you knew that was what I wanted.

One morning I thought, Why must I make a choice? Why can't I have both you and the depths? Would that be asking too much?

All day the thought burned in my mind.

That evening I asked you to marry me. I said it very simply: "Rachel, I want you to be my wife."

You looked out at the ocean, and you were silent for a long while, your face flushed.

Then you murmured, "I—I want to marry you, Eric, but are you asking me to marry an explorer or a teacher?"

"Can't an explorer marry, too?"

"Yes, an explorer can marry, but what would it be like? Don't you see, Eric? You'd be like Mark. Gone for maybe two months, maybe two years. Then you'd have a forty-eight hour leave—and I'd have what?"

Somehow I'd expected words like these, but still they hurt. "I wouldn't have to be an explorer forever. I could try it for a couple of years, then teach."

"Would you, Eric? Would you be satisfied with just seeing the Tonga Trench? Wouldn't you want to go on to the Kermadec and the Philippine Trenches and on and on?"

Your voice was choked, and even in the dim light I saw tears in your eyes.

"Do you think I'd dare have children, Eric? Justin told me what happened on the Cyclops expedition. There was a leak in the reactor. The submarine was flooded with radiation—just for a second. It didn't seem serious. The crew had no burns. But a year later the captain had a child. And it was—"

"I know, Rachel. Don't say it."

You had to finish. "It was deformed."

That night I lay awake, the fears and doubts too frantic to let me sleep.

You've got to decide now, I told myself. You can't stay here. You've got to make a choice.

The teaching job was still open. The spot on the Mariana Explorer was still open—and the big ship, it was rumored, was equipped to reach the deepest point in any ocean.

You can take Dean Page's job and stay with Rachel and have children and a home and live to see what happens in this world sixty years from now.

Or you can see what's at the bottom of the trench. You can be a line in a history book.

I cursed. I knew what Mark would say. He'd say, "Get the hell out of there, kid. Don't let fear make a coward out of you. Get out there on the Mariana Explorer where you belong. We got a date at the Tonga station, remember? At the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay."

That's what he'd say.

And yet I wanted you, Rachel. I wanted to be with you, always.

"Oh God," I moaned, "what shall I do?"

Next morning the door chimed, and you went to the door and brought back the message tablet. It was addressed to me; I wondered who could be sending me a message here at your family's home in Westfield.

I pressed the button on the small device, and a synthetic, automatic voice droned: "Tonga Deep-Sea Station, June 28, 2045. Regret to inform you of death of Mark Rogers, Chief Engineer...."

Then there was a medical term which was more clinical than the word "pressure-lung" and the robotic phrase, "This message brought to you by courtesy of International Deep-Sea Communication Network."

I stood staring at the tablet.

Mark Rogers was dead.

Mark Rogers was Deep-Sea Mark.

My heart thudded crazily against my chest. It couldn't be! Not Mark! The message had lied!

I pressed the button again. "...regret to inform you of death of Mark..."

I hurled the tablet at the wall. It clattered, fell, skidded. The broken voice droned on.

You ran to it, shut it off. "I'm sorry, Eric, so terribly—"

Without answering, I walked into my room. I knew it was true now. I remembered Mark's coughing, his gaunt features, his medicated gaze. The synthetic words had told the truth.

I sat for a long time on my bed, crying inside, but staring dry-eyed at Mark's weathered metal box.

Then, finally, I examined his meager possessions—a few faded photos, some letters, a small carved sculpture from the Mariana Trench, a service medal from the Atlantic Abyss operations.

This was what remained of Mark after thirty years in the depths. It was a bitter bargain. A sculpture instead of a wife, yellowed letters instead of children, a medal instead of a home.

It'd be a great future, I thought. You'd dream of sitting in a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station with pressure-adapted fish swimming past murky viewports. A bottle of kelp liquor and a couple of depth-workers with weathered faces for company. And a sudden cough that would be the first sign of pressure-lung.

To hell with it!

I walked into your living room and called Dean Page on the videophone. The connection routed back to the Institute in Prandoria, and her face appeared on the screen.

I accepted that job teaching.

And now, Rachel, it's nearly midnight. You're in your room, sleeping, and the house is silent.

It's hard to tell you, to make you understand, and that is why I am writing this.

I looked through Mark's box again, more carefully this time, reading the old letters and studying the photographs. I believe now that Mark sensed my indecision, that he left these things so that they could tell me what he could not express in words.

And among the things, Rachel, I found a ring.

A wedding ring.

In that past he never talked about, there was a woman—his wife. Mark was young once, his eyes full of dreams, and he faced the same decision that I am facing. Two paths were before him, but he tried to travel both. He later learned what we already know—that there can be no compromise. And you know, too, which path he finally chose.

Do you know why he had to medicate himself to watch me graduate? So he could look at me, knowing that I would see the depths he could never live to explore. Mark didn't leave just a few trinkets behind him. He left himself, Rachel, for he showed me that a young person's dream can also be an adult's dream.

He made his last trip to Tonga when he knew he was going to die. Heaven knows how he escaped a medical checkup. Maybe the captain understood and was compassionate—but that doesn't matter now.

Do you know why he wanted to reach the Tonga Trench? Do you know why he didn't want to die in the clean, safe air of the surface?

It was because he wanted to die nearer home. His home, Rachel, was the Ocean, where the submarine was his house, the crew his family, the trenches his children.

You say that the beauty of the unknown vanishes after you reach it. But how can one ever be sure until the journey is made? Could I or Mark or the thousand before us bear to look upon a trench and think, I might have gone there; I could have been the first?

We said, too, that the life of an explorer is lonely. Yet how could one be lonely when people like Mark roam the depths?

Mark wanted me to himself that night after graduation. He wanted us to celebrate as explorers should, for he knew that this would be his last night on the surface. It might have seemed an ugly kind of celebration to you, but he wanted it with all his heart, and we robbed him of it.

Because of these things, Rachel, I will be gone in the morning. Explain the best you can to Justin and to your parents and Dean Page.

Right now I've got a date that I'm going to keep—at a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay.

Deep-Sea Mark will be there; he'll go with me in memory to whatever part of the Ocean I may live to explore. And so will you, Rachel.

I have two wedding rings with me—his wife's ring and yours.
